name: Question 13
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226336/assets/3aa82e021a1871bd17abfd72570452bc6aefe358a8fddd3cb8e92bb6ff91c5a9.png)

The area of one loop of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{3})$ (shown above) is given by the integral

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?
worked_solution:
The given polar curve is the polar rose with $2\cdot 2=4$ petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is

$$
A={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{\pi /3}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226336/assets/3aa82e021a1871bd17abfd72570452bc6aefe358a8fddd3cb8e92bb6ff91c5a9.png)

The $1$st petal is traversed from ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{6}$ to ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{3},$ and the length of this interval is $\frac{\pi }{2}.$

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{3} & ={\theta }_{1}+\frac{\pi }{2}=-\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{3} \\ {\theta }_{4} & ={\theta }_{2}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{5} & ={\theta }_{3}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6} \\ {\theta }_{6} & ={\theta }_{4}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{4\pi }{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add $\frac{\pi }{2}$ to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\theta }_{7} & ={\theta }_{5}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{5\pi }{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{4\pi }{3} \\ {\theta }_{8} & ={\theta }_{6}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{4\pi }{3}+\frac{\pi }{2}=\frac{11\pi }{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all $4$ petals of our rose:

$$
{{[-\frac{\pi }{6},\frac{\pi }{3}]}_{⏟}}_{1\text{st}},\,{{[\frac{\pi }{3},\frac{5\pi }{6}]}_{⏟}}_{2\text{nd}},\,{{[\frac{5\pi }{6},\frac{4\pi }{3}]}_{⏟}}_{3\text{rd}},\,{{[\frac{4\pi }{3},\frac{11\pi }{6}]}_{⏟}}_{4\text{th}}
$$

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from $\theta =-\frac{\pi }{6}$ to $\theta =\frac{11\pi }{6}:$

$$
{A}_{\text{total}}={\int }_{-\pi /6}^{11\pi /6}{sin}^{2}⁡(2\theta +\frac{\pi }{3})\,\text{d}\theta 
$$

Question 13
?

The area of one loop of the polar curve r=2sin⁡(2θ+π3) (shown above) is given by the integral A=∫−π/6π/3sin2⁡(2θ+π3)dθ. Which of the following represents the total area bounded by the polar curve?

a
32∫π/211π/6sin2⁡(2θ+π3)dθ
b
∫−π/64π/3sin2⁡(2θ+π3)dθ
c
∫−π/611π/6sin2⁡(2θ+π3)dθ
d
∫−π/65π/6sin2⁡(2θ+π3)dθ
e
12∫π/34π/3sin2⁡(2θ+π3)dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The given polar curve is the polar rose with 2⋅2=4 petals, and we know that the area of the first petal is A=∫−π/6π/3sin2⁡(2θ+π3)dθ.

The 1st petal is traversed from θ1=−π6 to θ2=π3, and the length of this interval is π2.

To find the interval for the second petal, we have to add π2 to both ends of the interval of the first petal:

θ3=θ1+π2=−π6+π2=π3θ4=θ2+π2=π3+π2=5π6

Next, to obtain the interval for the third petal, we add π2 to both ends of the interval of the second petal:

θ5=θ3+π2=π6+π2=5π6θ6=θ4+π2=5π6+π2=4π3

Finally, to obtain the interval for the fourth petal, we add π2 to both ends of the interval of the third petal:

θ7=θ5+π2=5π6+π2=4π3θ8=θ6+π2=4π3+π2=11π6

Consequently, we obtain the following intervals for all 4 petals of our rose: [−π6,π3]⏟1st,[π3,5π6]⏟2nd,[5π6,4π3]⏟3rd,[4π3,11π6]⏟4th

Therefore, the total area of the given polar curve can be obtained if the curve is traversed from θ=−π6 to θ=11π6:

Atotal=∫−π/611π/6sin2⁡(2θ+π3)dθ
